For a month Ines had accepted every excuse. Abebe had a headache on the day of the class trip to Sintra. He was "too tired" for his friend's birthday. He wanted to skip football because "the coach is annoying". Each time she said, "Okay, stay home," partly because arguing upset him so much and partly because the house was calmer.
Then on Friday he asked her to phone the pharmacy for him, something he used to do easily. Her stomach sank. The excuses weren't about headaches. His world was shrinking, and she had been helping it shrink.
That evening she didn't push and didn't rescue. She sat on his bed. "I think things feel scary lately. I'm not going to make you do everything. But let's pick one small thing this week. You choose."
Abebe was quiet for a long time. "Maybe football. Just the warm-up."
"Just the warm-up," she agreed. "I'll wait in the car."

qa.q: What did Abebe ask Ines to do for him on Friday?
qa.a: Phone the pharmacy for him.

qa.q: What did Ines feel when Abebe asked her to phone the pharmacy?
qa.a: She felt a sinking worry, realising the excuses hid fear and that her kindness had been helping his world shrink.

qa.q: Why is Ines's new approach better than pushing or rescuing?
qa.a: She acknowledges the fear and invites one small, chosen step, so Abebe builds courage without being forced or shielded.

qa.q: What might Abebe be feeling when he chooses the warm-up?
qa.a: He likely feels nervous but a little relieved, since the step is small and he got to choose it.

grounding: A mother notices she has been accepting excuses and accommodating her son's fear, and shifts to kindly encouraging one small step.

In the school counsellor's small office, Naveen sat on a plastic chair and listed it all: Jaya had missed the science exhibition, the Annual Day rehearsal and two class tests this term. Each time she'd had a stomach ache, and each time he or her mother had written a note.
"She gets so upset," he said. "Honestly, it was easier."
The counsellor nodded. "That's very common. Parents want to protect. But each time she avoids, the fear grows a little."
Naveen looked at his hands. He remembered Jaya at eight, singing on stage, and felt a sharp stab of guilt.
Together they made a plan. No more notes for stomach aches unless the doctor advised it. Instead, small steps: Jaya would sit the next test but could take a seat near the door. Naveen would drive her and wait in the car park the first week, then only drop her off.
Walking out, he felt nervous, but clearer than he had in months.

qa.q: What did Jaya miss this term?
qa.a: The science exhibition, the Annual Day rehearsal and two class tests.

qa.q: What did Naveen feel remembering Jaya singing on stage at eight?
qa.a: He felt a sharp stab of guilt, seeing how the easy notes had helped her fear grow.

qa.q: What makes the new plan wise?
qa.a: It stops rescuing with notes but offers kind, small steps, like a seat near the door and a waiting father at first, so Jaya builds confidence.

qa.q: What might Jaya feel when she hears the plan?
qa.a: Jaya may feel scared and a bit upset, but also safer knowing her father will be close at first.

grounding: A father realises he has accommodated his daughter's fear with notes, and with a counsellor plans kind, small steps instead.

Dear Chandrika,
I'm writing because when we talk, I either say too much or nothing.
Over the last months I've said yes every time you wanted to skip something: the class picnic, your cousin's engagement, the badminton trials. I told myself I was keeping the peace. Truthfully, I didn't want to see you upset, and I didn't want to be the bad guy. But I've watched the list of places you can go get shorter, and I think my yeses helped make it shorter.
I'm not going to drag you anywhere. That wouldn't help either. But I'd like us to try one small thing each week, something you pick. Maybe it's just coming with me to the market on Sunday and buying the vegetables yourself. If it's hard, tell me, and we'll still count it as a try.
I'm proud of how hard you're working at this, even when it doesn't look like it.
Your Papa,
Ramesh

passage:
Last winter, before my board exams, I must have asked Mummy the same question fifty times a day. "Will I pass? Are you sure? What if I blank out?" She'd say, "You'll be fine," and for about five minutes I'd feel okay. Then the worry would crawl back and I'd ask again, sometimes in the same sentence.
I also checked my admit card every night. Twice. Then once more after brushing my teeth. I messaged Imran: "Did you also study chapter 7? Are you sure it's in the syllabus?" He answered patiently, then less patiently.
The strange part is that every answer helped less than the one before. It was like drinking salt water. And somewhere deep down I started to believe I couldn't calm myself at all, that only someone else's "you'll be fine" could do it.
I'm Chinmay, and I didn't see the pattern until my mother gently stopped answering.

qa.q: How many times did Chinmay check the admit card each night?
qa.a: Twice. Then once more after brushing my teeth.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel after each reassurance?
qa.a: Chinmay felt calm for about five minutes, then anxious again, as each answer helped less than the last.

qa.q: What would help Chinmay more than more reassurance?
qa.a: Noticing the worry, sitting with it for a while without asking, and learning it can ease without someone else's answer.

qa.q: How might Imran feel answering the same questions?
qa.a: Imran likely feels patient at first, then tired and a little frustrated, unable to settle the worry for good.

grounding: A teen repeatedly asks for reassurance and rechecks worries, gaining brief relief but learning that the mind cannot cope alone.

School counsellor's note, 5 September
Aparna, Class 9, was referred by her class teacher, Ms Elizabeth, who noticed she asks the same question several times every period: "Is this going to be in the test? Are you sure?" Her mother told me on the phone that at home Aparna asks whether the door is locked, whether the gas is off and whether she will pass, up to twenty times an evening.
In our session Aparna said, "When someone says it's fine, I feel better. Then it starts again." She looked embarrassed. She said she hates asking but can't stop, and that she's scared she is "too weak to handle things on her own".
I explained that reassurance calms worry for a moment yet leaves the mind believing it always needs someone else. We agreed on an experiment: she will write the worry in a notebook and wait ten minutes before asking. Her mother will answer once, kindly, and then say, "You've got this."
Review in two weeks.

qa.q: Who referred Aparna to the counsellor?
qa.a: Her class teacher, Ms Elizabeth.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when she said she's too weak to handle things alone?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and anxious, stuck in a loop where each reassurance helps only briefly.

qa.q: What experiment did the counsellor suggest, and why?
qa.a: Writing the worry down and waiting ten minutes before asking, with one kind answer from her mother, so Aparna learns she can cope.

qa.q: What might Ms Elizabeth have noticed in class?
qa.a: She noticed Aparna asking the same question every period and felt concerned enough to refer her.

grounding: A counsellor notes a teen who asks the same worried questions again and again, easing fear briefly but learning she cannot cope alone.

I asked Jomon chettan five times today if the college fair next week will be okay. Five. He said yes every time. After the fifth he said, "Reena, you already know what I'll say."

In their town near Cuttack, Kamal had run the family's small cloth shop since his father fell ill. Every evening he locked the shutter, walked away, then came back to rattle the padlock. Once. Twice. On bad nights, five times, with the tea-stall owner watching.
When he had to go to the post office to send the monthly parcel, he rehearsed his sentences under his breath all the way: "One parcel to Bhubaneswar, registered, please." He made his sister Ira come along, though she had her own college work.
Each time nothing went wrong, and for a moment he felt calm. Then the thought came: it was fine because I checked, because Ira was there. Without that, who knows?
On Friday Ira said, "Bhai, I have an exam. Go alone." Kamal stood at the post office door for ten minutes, rehearsing, heart pounding, before he could make himself step inside.

qa.q: How many times did Kamal rattle the padlock on bad nights?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling at the post office door?
qa.a: He felt anxious and exposed, heart pounding without Ira, because his safety habits had convinced him he couldn't manage alone.

qa.q: What could help Kamal loosen these habits?
qa.a: Check the lock once and walk on, go to the post office without rehearsing every word, and notice that nothing bad happens.

qa.q: What is it like for Ira to be needed everywhere?
qa.a: Ira cares about her brother but feels stretched, torn between her exam and his fears.

grounding: A young shopkeeper rechecks locks, rehearses lines and brings his sister along; each habit calms him briefly but makes the task feel dangerous.

For the first month Jatin didn't attend my lectures at all; his friend Nandini told me that crowded halls made him panic. In week five he appeared in the very back row, Nandini right beside him.
Over the following weeks I watched her quietly move. In week seven she sat one seat away. In week nine, two rows ahead, turning once to give him a thumbs-up. In week eleven she came in late on purpose, and he had already found his own seat near the middle.
After each class I heard her say something specific: "You stayed the whole hour." "You asked a question today." Never grand praise, only the effort.
Last Thursday Jatin came alone and answered a question in front of eighty students. Nandini was in the library. I'm recording this because it is the best example of support I have seen this year.

qa.a: Two rows ahead.

qa.q: Why did Nandini's gradual moving away help?
qa.a: Reducing her help step by step while praising his effort let Jatin build his own confidence.

qa.q: What might Jatin feel answering a question alone?
qa.a: He probably felt nervous but proud, realising he could manage the hall without Nandini beside him.

Ines had avoided phone calls for three years. In her small flat in Madrid she ordered food online, emailed her landlord and texted her dentist. When her new job required calls to suppliers, she panicked.
So one Sunday, with Santiago's coffee going cold beside her, she made a list. At the bottom, easiest: call the pizza place to ask their hours. Then: call her aunt. Then: book the dentist by phone. At the top: call a supplier.
On Monday she dialled the pizza place. Her heart thudded; her voice shook on the first hello. The man gave her the hours and hung up. Nothing terrible happened. She sat with her racing pulse for three minutes until it slowed.
She did the pizza call again on Tuesday, then called her aunt on Thursday. Each time the fear peaked, then faded. By the second week three lines had ticks, and the supplier call no longer looked like a cliff.

"That's the second time," Nirmala said. "What happened?"

"Then they'll tell you. That's their job, not yours."
Sunaina was quiet. "Will you sit with me while I call to rebook?"

Nitin, you asked what Chhath is like. Okay, imagine this. Four in the morning, still dark, and our whole mohalla is walking to the river in Patna. Dadi carries the bamboo basket on her head, full of thekua and bananas and sugarcane. I carry the diya and try not to let it go out.
At the ghat the water is freezing. Dadi and Mummy stand in it up to their waists, facing east, and we all wait for the sun. Everybody sings the same songs I've heard since I was a baby. When the sun finally comes up, orange, everyone offers arghya together, and I get goosebumps every single time.
I don't really think about why we do it. It's just ours. It's Dadi's hand on my head afterwards, and thekua that tastes better than anything, and all my cousins in one place.
I'm Ganga, by the way, named after a river. So I suppose I was always going to love this festival.

Three days before Losar. Pema helped her grandmother fold white khadas and polish the brass bowls for the altar. Ama-la showed her how to fill seven bowls with water, left to right, without spilling a drop. Pema didn't ask why seven. It was simply how it had always been.
Losar eve. The whole family climbed to the monastery above Gangtok. Pema spun the prayer wheels on the way up, one after another, the way her father had shown her when she was small. Inside, the monks chanted, butter lamps flickered, and she sat squeezed between her cousins, sleepy and happy.
Losar day. Rashmi from her class came over for the first time. Pema proudly showed her the altar and handed her khapse, the fried sweet biscuits. "What do the bowls mean?" Rashmi asked.
Pema opened her mouth, then laughed. "Honestly? I don't know. We just do it. It's home."

qa.q: How many water bowls did Pema fill?
qa.a: Seven bowls.

qa.q: What does Pema's laugh at Rashmi's question reveal?
qa.a: Pema feels warm and secure in the tradition, surprised to realise she has never questioned it because it simply feels like home.

grounding: Over the days of a festival a teen takes part in family rituals that feel warm, unquestioned and tied to belonging.

Simran, you asked why I still keep this tulsi mala in my pocket. Let me tell you about me at fourteen.
Every year, in the rains, my father and I walked with the wari to Pandharpur. Eighteen days on foot, with thousands of pilgrims singing abhangs, drums and cymbals, dust and mud. I didn't wonder whether Vitthal was listening. I didn't wonder anything. My feet hurt, my father's hand was on my shoulder, and an old woman from the next village fed me bhakri every evening as if I were her own grandson.
When we finally saw the temple spire, everyone wept and danced, and I did too, without knowing why. It was the happiest I have ever been.
Faith, for me then, was that crowd, my father's voice singing beside me, and that old woman's bhakri. That is what I still carry. I'm Nilesh; the questions came later, but that belonging never left.

qa.q: How many days did the walk to Pandharpur take?
qa.a: Eighteen days on foot.

qa.q: What did young Nilesh feel when the temple spire came into view?
qa.a: He felt overwhelming joy and belonging, weeping and dancing without needing to know why.

qa.q: What choice inside the story shaped Nilesh's faith?
qa.a: His father's choice to take him on the wari every year, which tied faith to walking together, singing and being fed by strangers.

qa.q: How might the old woman who fed Nilesh have seen him?
qa.a: She probably saw him as a young pilgrim to care for like her own grandson, sharing her bhakri out of kindness and devotion.

grounding: An elder recalls a teenage pilgrimage where faith was warm, unquestioned and bound up with family and community belonging.

In the biology lab, Rukmini ma'am drew the tree of life on the board: bacteria at the root, then fish, reptiles, mammals branching upward. "Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor," she said.
Aditi's pen stopped. At home her grandmother told stories every night about how the world was made, and Aditi had never once doubted them. She loved those stories. She had drawn pictures of them as a child.
She raised her hand, then lowered it. What would she even ask? And what if her grandmother found out she'd asked?
After class she lingered. "Ma'am, can both be true? The science and the stories my family believes?"
Rukmini ma'am put down the chalk. "Many people hold both, in different ways. It's a good question, and it's yours to think about."
Aditi nodded, but her stomach stayed tight all the way home. That night, when her grandmother began the usual story, Aditi felt a small, guilty flicker of doubt, and quickly pushed it away.

qa.q: What did Rukmini ma'am draw on the board?
qa.a: The tree of life.

qa.q: What did Aditi feel when the flicker of doubt came during her grandmother's story?
qa.a: She felt guilty and anxious, worried about disappointing her grandmother by even questioning.

qa.q: What could help Aditi with this new question?
qa.a: Keep asking gently, perhaps talk with her grandmother about what the stories mean to her, and treat the question as allowed, not shameful.

qa.q: How might Rukmini ma'am see Aditi's question?
qa.a: She sees it as thoughtful and normal, respecting both the science and Aditi's family beliefs.

grounding: A science lesson raises a first question about a teen's inherited beliefs, and she feels guilt and fear about disappointing her grandmother.

Dear Amandeep bhaiya,
I don't know who else to write to. You know Rohini, my friend from tuition? She died last month when the school bus went off the hill road. She was fifteen. She prayed more than anyone I know; she wore her red thread every single day.
At the funeral everyone kept saying it was God's will. I nodded. But inside I kept thinking: why would God want that? I've always believed that if you pray, you're protected. Now I don't know.
I haven't said this to Mummy or Dadi. They go to the temple every morning, and I still go with them, but I just stand there. I feel so guilty even writing this, like I'm betraying them. What if they think I'm turning away from everything they taught me?
You moved abroad and still come back for Diwali every year. Did you ever have questions like this? How did you live with them?
Ganga

qa.a: Ganga feels guilty and afraid, worried that questioning prayer after Rohini's death betrays the family's faith.

qa.a: Amandeep would likely feel moved and protective, honoured to be trusted with Ganga's grief and doubt.

Chandrika, can I tell you something that's been bothering me? Every Sunday at our satsang, Guruji says we're all the same soul, that no one is higher or lower. Everyone nods. My mother nods the hardest.
And then we go home, and the lady who cleans our house drinks from a separate steel glass that sits on its own shelf. I never noticed it before. It was just always there. This week I noticed, and now I can't stop seeing it.
So which is true? The satsang or the shelf? I asked Mummy, very carefully, and she said, "Don't ask such things, it's how it's always been." She looked hurt, as if I'd accused her.
Now I feel terrible. I love the bhajans. I love sitting next to Nani at satsang. I don't want to be the girl who ruins it by asking. But I'm Rukmini, and I can't un-see that glass.

qa.a: She feels guilty and torn, afraid of hurting her mother and spoiling what she loves, yet unable to ignore the contradiction.

October. In her first term in Delhi, Madhuri still went to Sunday mass at the cathedral, alone, taking two metros. She lit a candle for her grandfather and texted her mother a photo of it.
January. Exams, then a cold snap. She skipped mass three Sundays running and stayed in bed reading. Her roommate Binita, who had grown up in a family with no religion at all, lent her a book of essays about doubt. Madhuri read it in two nights, heart racing, as if doing something forbidden.
March. On Easter Sunday Madhuri didn't go. She sat on the hostel terrace with Binita, arguing happily about meaning and whether anyone needs God to be good. It felt free, like opening a window. Then her mother called, voice bright, asking which mass she had attended. Madhuri said, "The morning one," and hung up feeling hollow. The old certainty was loosening, and she already missed it.

qa.q: What did Binita lend Madhuri?
qa.a: A book of essays about doubt.

qa.q: What did Madhuri feel after telling her mother she'd attended mass?
qa.a: She felt hollow and guilty, missing the old certainty even as the new freedom felt good.

qa.q: What could Madhuri try instead of saying 'the morning one'?
qa.a: Tell her mother gently that she's thinking through questions, so honesty keeps them close even as her beliefs shift.

qa.a: Binita enjoys the lively debates and is happy to share books, perhaps without realising how much the loss weighs on Madhuri.

grounding: Over months away from home a young woman skips mass, reads widely and befriends a non-believer, feeling freedom and loss together.

Farhan, you said you've stopped going to Friday prayers since you moved here, and you feel both lighter and lost. I know that feeling. Let me tell you about Omkar at twenty.
I grew up in a village where my grandfather rang the temple bell every dawn, and I rang it with him. When I came to college in Pune, I stopped. Nobody told me to. I just started reading: economics and philosophy in the library, the Gita with a professor who questioned everything, Kabir's poems. My friends were a Parsi boy, a Christian girl from Goa and a canteen cook who fed us free when we were broke, all believing different things.
My certainty cracked. I felt free, like a bird out of a cage. But the first time I went home and heard that dawn bell, I sat on the step and cried, and I didn't know if I was crying for God or for my grandfather.
That was the day I decided I didn't have to choose at once. You don't either.

qa.a: In Pune.

qa.q: What did young Omkar feel crying on the step?
qa.a: Young Omkar felt a painful mix of freedom and loss, unsure whether the tears were for God or for a grandfather.

qa.q: What choice did young Omkar make on the temple step?
qa.a: To stop forcing an answer and allow both the freedom and the loss, deciding there was no need to choose at once.
